stories.headline: Rookie Luis Lara's latest web gem helps Brewers hold off Cubs
stories.summary: Brewers rookie outfielder Luis Lara added to what's already a season's worth of highlights in just two months with a leaping grab at the wall in right-center.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Milwaukee Brewers rookie outfielder Luis Lara has made a season's worth of spectacular plays in two months since getting called up to the big leagues.

And he has made most of them while playing a position that's new to him.

The latest one came Monday afternoon and helped the Brewers preserve a 4-3 victory over Chicago that enabled them to extend their NL Central lead over the Cubs to eight games.

Milwaukee led 4-2 when Lara used all of his 5-foot-7 frame to make a leaping catch of Pedro Ramirez's drive that otherwise would have left the park or hit the top of the wall in right-center.

"Really, in that situation, I'm just reacting," Lara said through interpreter Daniel de Mondesert. "That's the only thing going through my head is reacting to the play, to the ball off the bat, and just finding any way I possibly can to make the play there."

Considering that Pete Crow-Armstrong homered immediately afterward to cut Milwaukee's lead to one, Lara's catch essentially kept the Cubs from tying the game.

"Lara made a great catch there -- incredible play," Ramirez said through interpreter Fredy Quevedo Jr.

But it wasn't an unusual play, at least as far as Lara is concerned. He has demonstrated a flair for making amazing catches in critical situations since making his major league debut exactly two months ago.

Lara crashed against the right-field wall to catch Kody Clemens' drive and prevent Minnesota from scoring in the 10th inning of the Brewers' 4-3 win on Aug. 9. He also made another leaping play at the wall to prevent Brooks Lee from getting an extra-base hit earlier in that game.

Less than two weeks later, Lara robbed Matt Olson of an extra-base hit while playing center field in a 2-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves on Aug. 21.

Lara's willingness to go all out to make any play has endeared him to his new teammates.

"That's what we want from our outfielders and our defense, and that's the standard," said Brewers closer Trevor Megill, who was pitching when Lara made his ninth-inning catch Monday. "He goes out there and does that every single day on defense."

Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy also pointed out the 21-year-old's ability to handle adversity.

Lara, who is hitting .262 with a .696 OPS in 49 games, struck out to strand a runner on third and end the Brewers' three-run rally in the eighth inning Monday. Rather than stewing over that misstep, Lara immediately made up for it with remarkable defense.

"That response-type stuff is what it's all about," Murphy said. "Responding after things don't go right -- as quickly as possible."

The Brewers already were well aware of Lara's reputation as an outstanding fielder when he arrived in the majors. They signed him to a seven-year contract worth $31 million in guaranteed money when he was still in the minors.

Lara won a Gold Glove as one of the top three defensive outfielders in minor league baseball last year, when he was playing center field. He primarily has played right field since getting to Milwaukee, but he has continued producing defensive highlights.

"In right field, you have a little bit less time to maybe read the ball," he said. "You have to react a little bit quicker. In center field, I have maybe a little bit more time to think about the play or maybe to read the ball off the bat. Since I moved to right, it's all about reaction."

Lara's emergence gives Milwaukee an abundance of ideal defensive options in the outfield.

The Brewers closed Monday's game with three outfielders capable of playing center, as Lara was in right with Garrett Mitchell in the middle and Jackson Chourio in left. Sal Frelick gives the Brewers a 2024 Gold Glove right fielder who also has experience playing center.

Having so many outfielders with that kind of range provides Milwaukee's pitching staff with a sense of security. After Lara made his remarkable play in the ninth inning Monday, Chourio made a diving catch of Seiya Suzuki's fly to left for the final out.

Lara said he's fine playing anywhere in the outfield.

"I feel comfortable at all three outfield positions," he said. "I maybe didn't play a lot of right field in the minor leagues, but if they put me in left tomorrow, I think I'll feel comfortable. If they put me in center, I'll feel comfortable there. Wherever the team needs me, I'm comfortable in all three positions."

stories.headline: Fantasy football buzz: What Tua Tagovailoa being named starter means for Falcons
stories.summary: Matt Bowen looks at what Tua Tagovailoa starting means for Bijan Robinson, Drake London and Kyle Pitts Sr.
stories.body:
Everything that happens in the NFL has additional context when viewed from a fantasy football perspective. From position battles to injuries and so much more, the news cycle will constantly affect player values in fantasy football.

Our fantasy football buzz file, with contributions from our ESPN fantasy writers and our NFL Nation reporters, aims to provide fantasy managers with the intel they need as news breaks around the league.

Sept. 7: What Tua being named starter means for Falcons

By Matt Bowen

With the Atlanta Falcons naming Tua Tagovailoa as the starting quarterback for the Week 1 game versus the Pittsburgh Steelers, let's discuss the fantasy implications for head coach Kevin Stefanski's offense.

From a scheme perspective, Tagovailoa is a fit for what Stefanski wants at the position. A timing and rhythm thrower, Tagovailoa can be set up to throw with accuracy (68% career completion percentage) in a heavy play-action pass game. Look for deep in-breakers to Drake London here, along with the crossers and intermediate throws to tight end Kyle Pitts Sr. Plus, I do see Stefanski scripting isolation targets for both London and Pitts to generate positive matchups for Tagovailoa.

As it stands, Tagovailoa has some value in deeper 2QB Superflex formats. London will stay as a lower-tier WR1 in my ranks, while Pitts remains a midtier TE1 -- with breakout game ability.

In the Falcons' backfield, there is no change with Bijan Robinson. Stefanski's offense will cater to Robinson's dual-threat ability with high-end rushing volume and receiving opportunities. You can lock him as an elite RB1.

Sept. 4: Names to know in deep/keeper leagues before this weekend's draft

By Michael F. Florio

Drafting this weekend in a deep or a keeper league and need some names to keep in mind? In deep leagues, you are looking for stashes that have the chance to return value later in the season. In keeper leagues, you are looking for the same, but more so with players that could be values in drafts next year as well. Here are players that you should not forget about if you're in these types of leagues.

WR Jordyn Tyson was a middle-round pick before his hamstring injury. The New Orleans Saints first-round pick is extremely talented, with a playcaller in Kellen Moore who has run a pass-first offense in the past. He is a fantastic IR stash who could blossom into a second-half contributor. Those in keeper leagues should draft and stash, as he is sure to be more expensive next season.
Seattle Seahawks RB Zach Charbonnet is eligible to return in Week 5. He likely returns to RB3 value shortly thereafter and can be found in the late rounds.
Las Vegas Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza is not starting to open the season, meaning he is likely going to be undrafted in many formats. Still, the No. 1 pick is tied to a strong play caller and two elite offensive players (Brock Bowers, Ashton Jeanty) around him. He will play at some point and, if he hits, he will shoot up draft boards next season. Those are the kind of chances worth taking in the later rounds of keeper leagues.
Miami Dolphins QB Malik Willis can be found in the later rounds of drafts and brings QB1 upside. Here is the stat to know: Since 2000, 44 QBs have ran 100-plus times in a season, with 60% of them averaging 20 fantasy PPG. All but five averaged 17.4 points per game, which was the criteria to be a QB1 in fantasy last season.
WRs Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell are potentially the top targets for Willis in Miami this year. Douglas has received rave reviews from Dolphins camp and played every snap in preseason with Willis. Bell had first-round NFL Draft hype before he tore his ACL. Both have the upside to become weekly contributors.
Jacksonville Jaguars WR/CB Travis Hunter is simply a bet on talent. We are unsure what his role/usage will look like and, due to that, he can be had in the late rounds of drafts. He has the capability to be a weekly fantasy contributor if the offensive role is big enough. Plus, think of the hype in a keeper league if he hits!
Baltimore Ravens WR Ja'Kobi Lane has a chance to become the WR2 this season. His red zone capabilities on an offense led by Lamar Jackson means he has the potential to "touchdown his way" to fantasy relevance, even as the WR3. With a strong rookie showing, Lane could climb into the middle rounds of drafts next year, making him worth a late-round flier in keeper leagues.
San Francisco 49ers RB Kaelon Black played over Jordan James in the preseason and seems like the RB2 for the Niners. We have seen many backup backs become fantasy relevant under Kyle Shanahan. He has RB2 upside if Christian McCaffrey were to miss time.
Tennessee Titans RB Nicholas Singleton is more for those in keeper leagues. He likely will not contribute early, but we could see him take over as the season goes on. The key here is that both Titans RBs (Tony Pollard, Tyjae Spears) are free agents after the season.

Sept. 3: When to pick Swift and Odunze if you're drafting Thursday?

By Eric Moody

D'Andre Swift and Rome Odunze both left Chicago Bears practice Thursday with injuries, which creates some uncertainty for anyone drafting tonight.

Odunze appeared to injure his right leg early in practice. He reportedly tried to stay on the field and didn't seem overly concerned, but trainers eventually shut him down for the day. Swift left later after a carry while holding his midsection or core area and appeared to be in significant discomfort. The Bears have not provided an official diagnosis for either player yet.

So, what should you do if you're drafting tonight?

I'm not taking either player off my board, but ultimately it comes down to whatever your risk tolerance is.

Swift is currently the RB20 in ESPN leagues, while Odunze is the WR26. With so little information available, both could fall tonight as managers react to the news. If either player slips about a round past his usual draft spot -- Swift (51.7 ADP) and Odunze (64.9) -- I'd be willing to take him.

Swift carries a little more risk because of how uncomfortable he reportedly looked. Chicago is also dealing with an injury to Kyle Monangai, who is working his way back from a knee issue. If Swift were to miss Week 1 and Monangai wasn't ready, Roschon Johnson would be next in line. Odunze's situation sounds a little more encouraging. He tried to keep practicing before the training staff pulled him, and so far, there hasn't been anything suggesting the injury is serious.

If you draft either player, make sure you have another option you'd be comfortable starting in Week 1. Chris Godwin Jr. and Quentin Johnston are receivers available later in drafts with favorable Week 1 matchups, while Jordan Mason is an intriguing late round running back option. Aaron Jones Sr. and Mason had nearly identical preseason usage, which suggests they could split the rushing workload evenly this season.

If you don't like taking on injury risk, stay away.

But if your league starts pushing Swift or Odunze well past their normal draft range, you might want to be willing to take the discount. One round past ADP is where I'd be comfortable smashing the draft button on either player.

Sept. 1: Lions' Pacheco heads to IR, out four games

By Tristan H. Cockcroft

Signed in March to a one-year, $1.81 million deal to replace David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs' backfield partner/primary backup, Isiah Pacheco on Tuesday was placed on injured reserve by the Detroit Lions, ruling him out for the season's first four games. Pacheco had been dealing with an MCL sprain, but coach Dan Campbell raised more recent concerns about the 27-year-old's back, which ultimately led to the IR decision.

Pacheco's absence thrusts Gibbs, already a fantasy football superstar and the No. 1 player being picked on average in ESPN leagues, further into the spotlight. Already an explosive runner -- he's nicknamed "Sonic" for a reason -- Gibbs is also one of the game's best receiving running backs as well as a sound goal-line runner who has converted 11 of his 15 career chances into scores. There's little to quibble about with his game, and with his backup situation no longer completely clear, he could be in for the kind of workload that produces historic stat totals.

Though I have had Bijan Robinson ranked ahead of Gibbs all preseason, I've swapped them following this news. Gibbs now has a clear edge at the position.

As for that backup situation, zero-RB drafters can add a new name to their list of late-round candidates: Jacob Saylors. The former UFL standout averaged 6.0 yards per carry this preseason and took four of his 31 rushing attempts for 10-plus yards. Fantasy managers in ESPN standard leagues can monitor Saylors' usage in Week 1, as the Lions had previously leaned heavily upon Montgomery, but Saylors is beneath the roster-worthy threshold unless his workload is within range of that.

Aug. 30: What to know about the Packers' RB situation

By Eric Moody

The NFL placed Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs on the commissioner's exempt list Sunday after he was formally charged with misdemeanor battery and misdemeanor criminal damage to property. Jacobs has denied the allegations.

The commissioner's exempt list is an administrative move, not a suspension or a final ruling. Jacobs will continue to be paid, but he cannot practice or play while he's on the list and does not count against Green Bay's 53-man roster. There is no timetable for how long he'll remain on the list, and the NFL could still issue discipline later. That makes Jacobs difficult to value in fantasy drafts. There's no way to know how many games he might miss, and his placement on the exemption list does not make him eligible for the fantasy injured reserve list.

For now, it is safe to assume that MarShawn Lloyd will be the starting running back in Week 1 against the Minnesota Vikings. Green Bay also traded for Kaleb Johnson, who had 69 yards on 28 carries as a rookie in Pittsburgh. Lloyd has looked good this preseason and has worked with the starting offense, but durability remains the concern. Injuries have limited the 2024 third-round pick to just one career regular-season game. As long as Jacobs remains away from the team, Lloyd has a legitimate chance to lead this backfield. He should move up draft boards and immediately enters the flex conversation based on the volume alone. If I were drafting tonight, I'd be looking at Lloyd in Round 7 or 8, after Jadarian Price, Bhayshul Tuten and TreVeyon Henderson are off the board. I might still be willing to take Jacobs in the double-digit rounds, assuming my roster build can take on the risk. Lloyd's injury history also makes Johnson worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues where players such as Tank Bigsby and Dylan Sampson have marginal value.

Aug. 30: Aaron Donald returns to stacked Rams D/ST

By Adam Rank

Perhaps one of the worst-kept secrets in the NFL, kind of like when CM Punk returned to the WWE at Survivor Series 2023. We knew it was going to happen, we just weren't sure when. But Aaron Donald is back with the Los Angeles Rams. And a defense that was already pretty good has a chance to become elite. But what does this have to do with fantasy football? I'm glad you asked.

The Rams are currently listed at the D/ST No. 5 (173) in our ESPN Top 300 list. I know a lot of folks tend to think of D/ST as an afterthought. Something you draft at the very end of the draft, or sometimes not at all because you're going to stream a defense in Week 1. I'll even admit that I sometimes adhere to that strategy.

The Houston Texans are currently ranked as the top defense, followed by the Denver Broncos, Pittsburgh Steelers and Seattle Seahawks. The Rams should immediately jump to the top three. The Rams open with the San Francisco 49ers (Mac Jones beat them pretty well last year), New York Giants (intriguing) and the Broncos. But Los Angeles appears to be matchup-proof at this point, as this defensive line should be able to generate sacks and turnovers against some of the best defenses in the league.

Week 1 lookahead

All three of the top defenses have rather tough matchups out of the gate. The Texans have the Buffalo Bills and Cincinnati Bengals. The Broncos have the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.

Philosophy is the biggest thing here. Do you want to draft a defense you can set or forget? Or do you want to work to find the best option each week? For Week 1, you might look for the Jaguars (vs. Cleveland Browns) or Green Bay Packers (at Minnesota Vikings).

Aug 30: What I noticed on Saturday

By Adam Rank

The final weekend of NFL preseason can be rather uneventful. Most starters are on the bench. Many of the games feel like the opening act of a concert as you wait for the headliner. But here is what stood out on Saturday night.

Can we talk about Zavion Thomas? He caught all five of his targets for 140 yards and a 97-yard touchdown. He was even out there returning punts. Pretty much doing it all. This is great news for Bears fans. Ben Johnson has so many weapons to play with right now. It's going to be grueling for fantasy managers who are going to need to navigate this situation every week. We all know Luther Burden III has garnered the most headlines during the pre-draft season. Buzzing up draft boards. Watching Thomas could be a problem. In fact, the Bears still have Kalif Raymond, Ray-Ray McCloud and others who will get some significant targets. Even Sam Roush was showing out against the Titans in joint practices during the week. I've been telling folks if you want to get into the Bears business this year, you're probably safer taking Caleb Williams and enjoying the points, no matter who he is throwing the ball to. It's going to be very crowded.

Aug. 29: What you need to know from Friday's games

By Michael Florio

There were 10 NFL preseason games on Friday night, and though many teams did not dress their starters and used the game to figure out the back end of their rosters, some regulars were out there. Here are the key fantasy takeaways from those games and other happenings around the NFL.

Tua Tagovailoa started for the Atlanta Falcons and threw for 95 yards and a botched snap for a fumble. The Falcons have yet to name a starting QB. Those who draft Drake London might be hoping Michael Penix Jr. starts, as London averaged over 20 fantasy PPG with him last season. The star of the game was Kyle Pitts Sr., who turned three targets into 59 yards, including a 37-yard catch-and-run. Pitts brings a lot of upside with Kevin Stefanski, who targeted tight ends at the third-highest rate during his Cleveland Browns tenure.
Rookie receiver Makai Lemon got his first preseason action after missing time this preseason due to a hamstring injury. He finished with three catches for three yards on five targets. There is not much to take away, as the Philadelphia Eagles' regulars did not dress, but it was nice to see Lemon healthy again and back out there. He is an upside shot worth taking at his current ADP of WR52.

Miami Dolphins receivers Caleb Douglas and Malik Washington both sat with the starters, indicating they are atop the depth chart. While both are later-round fantasy picks, I have been taking Douglas in a lot of my drafts. He has been the star of Dolphins camp this summer. The story of the game last night was Chris Bell making his debut. Bell was expected to potentially go in the first round of the NFL draft before he tore his ACL. He finished with two catches for 22 yards on five targets. This was likely just him getting some work in as he returns from injury. It might take a few weeks for him to fully get up to speed, but there is potential here in the later rounds or as a waiver wire name this season. Dynasty players should take note.
The Kansas City Chiefs played their starting skill position players, with Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy operating in two-receiver sets. Tyquan Thornton, not Cyrus Allen, was the WR3. Running back Emmett Johnson started and saw the bulk of opportunities early on, turning seven carries and two targets into 54 total yards. Pending an outside addition, he appears locked in as Kenneth Walker III's insurance back.
New York Giants running back Devin Singletary did not dress for Friday's game, while Tyrone Tracy Jr. started and shared work with Najee Harris. This is a telling sign that Singletary is the current insurance back to draft behind Cam Skattebo.
Giants reporter Jordan Raanan wrote that it was likely that Malachi Fields starts the season as the No. 2 receiver, in part due to his size and blocking ability. Fields can be an immediate red zone weapon, which we have already seen in the preseason. He sat with the starters Friday night, while Darius Slayton and Odell Beckham Jr. both suited up. This puts Fields in the late-round range in 12-team leagues or deeper.
The Denver Broncos held out all their regulars, which included running backs RJ Harvey and rookie Jonah Coleman. Harvey is the high-upside RB2 worth drafting in the middle rounds. Coleman has clearly made a good impression and could take the lead role if J.K. Dobbins misses time. He is worth taking in the later rounds of drafts. Pat Bryant was also held out after running with the starters as the WR3 last week. He seems locked into that role to start the season. He is more of a dynasty stash to start the year.
Alec Pierce was activated off the PUP list and returned to practice Thursday. He said Friday that Week 1 was still his goal. When healthy, Pierce is one of the best field-stretchers in the NFL, having led the league in yards per catch each of the last two seasons. After signing the largest free agent wide receiver contract ever, a bump in usage could be coming his way. Pierce's WR36 ADP is a fair price given the risk and reward. I have been targeting him once I fill out my starting lineup and reach the reserve picks.
Raiders reporter Ryan McFadden believes Mike Washington Jr.'s play this preseason has changed the staff's perspective of the RB room. Ashton Jeanty is still an RB1 who should be drafted in the second round, but Washington is quickly climbing draft boards into the middle-round range. He is a top insurance back and could have standalone value.

Aug. 28: Who stood out Thursday night?

By Liz Loza

Pittsburgh Steelers at Buffalo Bills

The Steelers and Bills rested their top-tier starters, locking in both teams' premier fantasy talents. Buffalo started fourth-round rookie WR Skyler Bell, who had missed previous playing time while working through a groin issue. The 24-year-old UConn product put forth a solid debut effort, leading the offense in rushing and receiving. Bell excels at gaining separation via crafty route technique while compiling extra yardage courtesy of his change-of-direction ability. He projects as a slot or "Z" receiver at the next level. He's not expected to be a factor in redraft leagues, but his dynasty stock should be monitored.

New England Patriots at Cleveland Browns

Neither team's core starters suited up Thursday night. However, Patriots WR Kyle Williams continued to make noise. With Kayshon Boutte off to Houston, the speedy Washington State alum appears to have earned a spot on the team's 53-man roster. Williams hauled in his third touchdown grab of the preseason Thursday evening. He's battling with Mack Hollins and DeMario Douglas for No. 3 WR duties. Williams' presence as a vertical threat could lead to boom efforts, particularly in best-ball formats, but his overall profile doesn't offer much regular fantasy value.

San Francisco 49ers at Las Vegas Raiders

Leaning on the leg of Eddy Pineiro, San Francisco topped Las Vegas by a score of 18-12 in both teams' final preseason showing. Rookie sensation De'Zhaun Stribling sat, solidifying his regular-season starting status. Khalil Herbert led the squad in rushing, likely securing his role as a depth option behind Christian McCaffrey.

Klint Kubiak refused to state the obvious and officially name Kirk Cousins as the Raiders' Week 1 starter after the team's preseason loss to San Francisco. The vet took the field first, completing 8 of 11 attempts while leading the squad to two field goals. Fernando Mendoza followed shortly thereafter, tossing one pick and collecting two sacks. Clearly still in the developmental stage of his career, Mendoza remains a waiver wire option only in redraft and a high-investment hold in dynasty formats.

Fourth-round rookie Mike Washington Jr. stepped into the Raiders' RB1 role with Ashton Jeanty sidelined (ankle). The Arkansas product broke off numerous chunk gains early in the contest. In possession of 99th percentile speed (4.33), Washington is a high-motor RB who has the size and strength to break tackles while picking up extra yards after contact. He's firmly entrenched as the squad's RB2, offering elite backup value in the double-digit rounds of ESPN Fantasy drafts.

Los Angeles Rams at Los Angeles Chargers

Sean McVay rested the Rams' key starters. Jim Harbaugh, on the other hand, teased fantasy fans by briefly rolling out Justin Herbert. The QB completed 2 of 3 passes, losing a fumble and then connecting with Quentin Johnston on a gorgeous 65-yard touchdown. It's a positive sign for the team's aerial attack, now under the design of new OC Mike McDaniel. Herbert remains one of the virtual game's most intriguing values, offering top-10 positional upside in the 10th round of drafts. Meanwhile, Johnston, who appears fully recovered from a lower-body malady, endures as a late-round bounce-back candidate, worthy of being redeemed in an offense suited to explosive playmaking and YAC prowess.

Aug. 27: Why 49ers' Evans is worth taking at his current ADP

By Eric Moody

Managers got some encouraging news on Mike Evans this week. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported that Evans' recent groin injury is considered minor and that the 33-year-old plans to play in the San Francisco 49ers' Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Rams. Evans also dealt with a quad issue during training camp, however, so his health is still worth monitoring.

The good news is that some of that concern is already reflected in Evans' draft cost. Evans currently is being selected as the WR34 in ESPN leagues. At that price, you're not drafting the version of Evans who opened his career with 11 straight 1,000-yard seasons. You're also not paying for that version.

Evans has been one of the most consistent receivers of his generation, having accumulated 866 receptions for 13,052 yards and 108 touchdowns, with six seasons of double-digit scores. Last year was different. Injuries limited him to eight games, and his efficiency dipped. Evans ranked 49th in yards per route run and 55th in yards per catch. However, he averaged 7.5 targets and 12.7 fantasy points per game over the final four games of the season, showing that he's still a capable receiver at this stage of his career.

One thing I'll be looking for early on is his chemistry with quarterback Brock Purdy. Evans has missed enough practice time that the two haven't had much work together. It may take a little time before everything clicks.

The fit in San Francisco is also fascinating. Kyle Shanahan has gotten plenty out of his outside receivers over the years, and Evans could see more opportunities on in-breaking routes and over the middle of the field. He hasn't been used that way very often, but over the past six seasons he has averaged 3.47 yards per route run on in-routes.

The opportunity for targets should be there. Ricky Pearsall is out for the season, Brandon Aiyuk isn't expected to play for San Francisco and George Kittle is coming back from a torn Achilles. Evans has a legitimate chance to be one of Purdy's top targets, and our projections reflect that.

Touchdowns are where Evans can really pay off in fantasy. Purdy has a 6.2% touchdown rate since entering the league. Our own Mike Clay projects Evans for 101 targets -- most among 49ers players -- and six touchdowns. That would be solid production for a player being drafted as WR34.

Yes, there is the age factor. Since 2000, 73% of wide receiver seasons with at least 15 FPPG have come from players between the ages of 23 and 29. It's rare to see that type of production from a receiver Evans' age. Managers won't complain if Evans averages somewhere between 12 and 15 FPPG this season. That's within the realm of possibility if he stays healthy and capitalizes on his red zone opportunities.

You don't need Evans to look like he did five years ago for this pick to work. You're drafting him as a flex or WR3. If Evans stays on the field, there's a good chance he outperforms his average draft position.

Aug. 24: Streaming potential for Boutte in Houston

By Matt Bowen

On Monday, the Houston Texans traded for veteran wide receiver Kayshon Boutte, so let's discuss any fantasy implications from this deal.

Boutte scored 8.9 PPG last season in New England, posting double-digit production in five of 14 games played, which included the 26.3 points he dropped on the Saints in Week 6. He's a steady player on tape, one who displays route savvy, toughness and ball skills. However, Boutte lacks the speed to separate consistently, and he's not a true deep ball target.

Now, I get why Houston made the move here. Jayden Higgins went down last week with an ACL injury, plus Tank Dell -- who made a brief appearance earlier in camp -- is still recovering from a major knee injury at the end of the 2024 season. As of now, Boutte will be in competition for the No. 3 role with the Texans.

With the expected No.1 volume for Nico Collins and an improved Texans run game, Boutte most likely projects as a matchup-based streaming option this season.

Aug 24: How to monitor Jeanty if you're drafting Monday

By Matt Bowen

Fantasy managers went through it Sunday night with the news on Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty, who went down in practice with an injury. Original reports mentioned a potential knee injury as well as pointing out that Jeanty had to be helped off the field and couldn't put weight on the leg. However, with more updates, that injury in now considered a right ankle sprain, but the news is still pretty lean on a timetable for return, rehab and more.

While we wait for further reports, and most likely more testing on Jeanty's ankle, how do we approach this situation in Vegas?

Jeanty is currently my RB8 in the rankings, and I like the fit under new head coach Klint Kubiak behind an offensive line that added some players this offseason. He can finish as a top-five scorer at the position this season.

But if I'm in a league that is scheduled to draft Monday, well, I have to drop Jeanty a couple of spots into that RB10-12 range. And that seems fair knowing that Jeanty might not be ready for Week 1. Plus, we also have to mention Raiders' rookie running back Mike Washington Jr. The Arkansas product has flashed this preseason, showing his speed and contact balance to rip off explosive plays. The same stuff we saw on his SEC tape here. He can roll.

Washington should be targeted as a draftable player in 10- and 12-team leagues. In addition to being a prime insurance back (I would really try to land Washington if you draft Jeanty), the rookie could see No.1 volume in the opening week matchup versus the Miami Dolphins at home.

Yes, this is still a wait-and-see approach given Jeanty's uncertain status, and we will update the situation as more news rolls in.

Aug. 23: What you need to know from Saturday's games

By Adam Rank

It would figure that one of the most polarizing battles in the fantasy community is for the Dallas Cowboys' RB2 position. You have the Jaydon Blue truthers (myself included) and the others. And Blue had a monster game on Saturday ... OK, fine, it was pretty good. The numbers are the numbers. But Blue showed some good burst and then went full Ezekiel Elliott, hurdling a Cardinals defender. Was it enough to cement his spot as the No. 2 guy? I'm guessing not. Malik Davis also had his moments, including an 8-yard touchdown reception. So really, you have to pick your side and dive in.

Here are some other notes I picked up watching a full day of football:

Speaking of the Cowboys, Camden Brown continues to impress with a 70-yard reception. The Cowboys are loaded at receiver, and we might not see him get into the top five behind CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Ryan Flournoy and KaVontae Turpin. But dang, he's fun to watch.
RB Emmett Johnson is making it nearly impossible to handicap who is going to be the insurance play behind Kenneth Walker III in the Kansas City Chiefs' offense. Johnson logged 21 snaps to lead all Chiefs backs over Brashard Smith (19) and Emari Demercado (14). Smith and Johnson had two targets each.
TE Colston Loveland avoided injury on a blatant hip-drop on Saturday night. Let's go ahead and put the Chicago Bears' offensive stars in bubble wrap (which now includes Jahdae Walker) and see you in September. Also, Ben Johnson looked irked ... terrible for the Chicago players in practice this week, great for us.

Aug. 20: Despite injury scare, Tyler Warren's fantasy ceiling is still massive

Aug. 19: What does Alvin Kamara's injury mean for the rest of the Saints RB room?

By Tristan H. Cockcroft

New Orleans Saints RB Alvin Kamara suffered a sprained MCL in his knee during Tuesday's joint practice with the Dallas Cowboys, and while he reportedly suffered no tears in the joint, the veteran running back is expected to miss one month. That timetable takes him beyond the Saints' Week 1 game against the Detroit Lions, and considering the difficulties NFL players often have recovering from lengthier injury absences, it could put his availability into question deeper into September.

Kamara, 30, was a massive fantasy disappointment last season, a fourth rounder on average in ESPN leagues (and the RB14) who delivered his fewest fantasy points in a season (100.7, in 11 games). There were rumors he was a prospective trade candidate leading up to the November deadline, but subsequent reports that he preferred to remain in New Orleans to finish out his career quashed those. The Saints then held him out of their final six games due to ankle and knee issues.

New Orleans subsequently signed Travis Etienne Jr. -- a top-10 scoring running back in two of the past three years (2023, 2025) -- to a four-year, $52 million contract of which $24 million is guaranteed, at the time giving the team one of the league's most expensive backfields (the team since reworked Kamara's contract). Kamara's early absence now vaults Etienne into the clear starter/three-down back role, something Etienne desperately needs if he's to repeat last year's RB10 finish in what's a significantly weaker offense than the one in which he played in Jacksonville.

Etienne is going 19th among running backs somewhere in the fifth round on average in early ESPN drafts, but the news strengthens his case for fantasy RB2 status. I had already slotted him ahead of Cam Skattebo as my No. 18 running back in the rankings, which is the opposite of how they're going in early drafts. Between this news and Najee Harris' arrival in New York on Tuesday, Etienne should be the superior pick between the two.

As for Kamara, he was generating reserve/late-round interest in early drafts, going 44th at the position. I've been down on him more than most, as he's now 31 years old with an average 3.8 games missed across the past five seasons, and the Saints made it clear late last year that they were fine with slotting him into a supporting role. This news doesn't make Kamara a non-factor in drafts, but he's sure to teeter around the No. 50 cutoff for our positional rankings, depending upon how I feel about the other sleepers around him over the next couple of weeks.

Incidentally, Kendre Miller and Devin Neal currently have the depth-chart advantage over Audric Estime, per the team's official release. But that signals a three-man competition for the No. 3 spot -- and now primary backup role -- meaning there's no clear insurance policy for Etienne to be had just yet. Look elsewhere for running back depth.

Aug. 18: Colts sign Keenan Allen, Giants adding Najee Harris

When Pierce does return, Allen could slide into the perimeter role that was held by Michael Pittman Jr. last season and also see reps in the slot, as Josh Downs can play inside or outside. And that works from a scheme perspective in Steichen's offense.

For me, Pierce remains an upside WR3 (with explosive play ability), while Tyler Warren stays as a high-end TE1. Nothing changes there. And I still value Downs as one of my later-round targets, while Allen should be viewed as a potential bench stash/streaming option based on Pierce's timeline and what we see next month.

Giants signing former Steelers RB Harris

Aug. 17: Jordyn Tyson to miss significant time

Aug. 17: Jeremiyah Love expected to miss rest of preseason

By Eric Karabell

Fantasy football managers (foolishly) want to see their top players perform in preseason games, but this is often only to the player's detriment, especially if a player boasts an established role. Injuries can happen to anyone. Arizona Cardinals RB Jeremiyah Love suffered a high ankle sprain against the Raiders on Thursday night, and it should affect his fantasy value. The problem is determining how much it should matter.

Great fantasy things were expected from Love, the No. 3 pick in the NFL draft out of Notre Dame, and they may still occur. Love curiously handled 14 touches in the preseason opener, accruing 72 yards. He averaged 5.3 yards per rush, with his longest going for 16 yards, and he caught three passes on three targets. Love sure looked like a fantasy star, and we covet running backs with potentially large workloads, but we can question why he was playing at all in a meaningless contest.

We will not see Love for the rest of the preseason, and it is plausible that he is compromised enough to miss September regular-season games as well. High ankle sprains can be mighty problematic in recovery time. Experts often use four to six weeks as a baseline, but we do not know the degree of this sprain. Love should be reevaluated this week, but the hopeful Cardinals are under no obligation to reveal specifics.

Love entered Monday morning as the No. 15 option overall in ESPN live drafts, a solid second-round selection, and ninth among running backs. However, this injury news should be enough to push him down a round, and out of the top 10 at the position, behind Baltimore's Derrick Henry, new Chief Kenneth Walker III and perhaps others.

We may find that it creates a solid value opportunity for drafting Love, for he might still play in Week 1 (Sept. 13) against the Chargers -- and he may play great. It is also possible Love may miss September and be affected by this injury for months. It's not like the Cardinals are expected to win the Super Bowl this season. They should be cautious and patient.

Former Atlanta Falcons bruiser Tyler Allgeier appears next in line for touches, especially with James Conner (foot) and Trey Benson (knee) not practicing. Allgeier, who rushed for 1,035 yards as a rookie in 2022 and then handled reserve duties behind superstar Bijan Robinson for three years, is not nearly as dynamic as Love, but he is certainly a capable fill-in, albeit not much of a pass-catching option. The physical Allgeier rushed for eight touchdowns last season, and he thrives running between the tackles. It is possible he would have carved out a significant role in this offense even with a healthy Love.

Some of this is guesswork as we lack clarity, but it is sensible to move Love down a few slots in the running back rankings, perhaps as far as the Javonte Williams and Kyren Williams range two rounds later in ADP. Also consider bumping Allgeier up to the point of being worth choosing in standard drafts. Perhaps fantasy managers will never need to utilize Allgeier, either because Love returns for Week 1 or because they don't need him, since NFL teams do not serve bye weeks in September, but injuries happen all season. Be prepared.

Lane is one of my favorite deep sleepers -- if he hasn't removed the "deep" label from that at this point -- who should improve the team's red zone deficiencies from 2025.
The Cleveland Browns gave us some fantasy-relevant returns ... yes, the Cleveland Browns! KC Concepcion caught 3 of 4 targets for 27 yards, but perhaps more importantly turned his lone rushing attempt into a 14-yard touchdown on an end-around. If the Browns are to continue to find creative ways to get their star rookie involved, he could provide WR3/flex value on a fairly regular basis, even from what projects to be one of the league's weaker offenses.

Aug. 13: Big opportunity for Jonathon Brooks; Jordyn Tyson injured

Brooks steps in while Hubbard is out

Brooks tore the ACL in his right knee twice over a span of 13 months. Currently 19 months removed from his second knee surgery, the 23-year-old has been a full participant in training camp. A versatile and instinctive three-down player at the position, Brooks is expected to carve out a significant role in Carolina's backfield.

Hubbard ceded command of the Panthers backfield to Rico Dowdle after dealing with a calf strain in Weeks 5 and 6 of last year. Carolina let Dowdle walk during the offseason, potentially freeing up 275 touches. While Hubbard is expected to begin the season as the team's RB1, there's a clear opportunity for Brooks to overtake the starting spot. Were Hubbard's hamstring issues to linger, Brooks' ascent could be fast-tracked. He's currently being drafted a round and a half after Hubbard, who is generally coming off boards in the middle of the 12th round (115).

Injuries already a concern for Saints rookie Tyson?

Jordyn Tyson reportedly left Thursday's practice early with what's believed to be a hamstring issue. Bi-lateral hamstring strains limited Tyson to nine games during his final season at Arizona State in 2025. Lingering soft tissue issues additionally forced the rookie to skip on-field workouts and physical testing at the NFL Combine earlier this year. Nonetheless, New Orleans selected the former Sun Devil No. 8 overall at the draft in April.

A versatile player with outstanding ball skills and route savvy, Tyson was expected to fill the Saint's No. 2 WR role, working as a dynamic complement to Chris Olave. The rookie had his reps managed during the team's offseason program and was medically cleared for training camp in late July. It's concerning that barely two weeks into practice, the hamstring issues have resurfaced. Were Tyson to miss time, Olave and Juwan Johnson would continue to lead the team in pass-catching opportunities.

Aug. 12: More volume for Chase Brown, Denzel Boston turning heads

By Cameron Wolfe

Big season coming for Chase Brown?

The Cincinnati Bengals will count on Brown to take on a heavier load this season with a focus on more under-center runs and usage in the pass game. Watching practice Sunday, it was eye-opening how much versatility the offense had with play formation and motion/shifts. It was a far cry from the Bengals' traditional shotgun-heavy, productive yet sometimes static offense. Brown will be the biggest beneficiary as a receiver and runner.

Joe Burrow said the team's No.1 priority is to get the ball in Ja'Marr Chase's hands but "a close second" is getting the ball to Brown.

Brown told me after practice, "I'm excited for it. There's going to be a lot of big plays we create."

Bengals head coach Zac Taylor told me he wants the Bengals to be prepared to go on lengthy, methodical touchdown drives rather than relying on deep shots defenses have prioritized stopping. The under-center focus isn't new -- they did it plenty in their Super Bowl season -- and one Bengals source said a key reason why there should be more snaps under center is to help keep Burrow healthy.

"Under center makes us a little more unpredictable," Brown said. "We have a lot of play-action and runs called from under center. When you're in I-formation, the ball can go either way. It keeps defenses on their heels more. If you look at the statistics from last year, almost all the most explosive run teams were majority under-center run teams. I look forward to continuing to build on that."

This is completely Brown's backfield in a contract year, so fantasy owners have plenty of reason to be confident in his heavy dual-threat usage, with eyes also on whether this focus limits the Bengals' secondary receiving weapons.

Denzel Boston: WR1 in Cleveland?

One Cleveland Browns source told me in camp last week that the rookie second-round wide receiver "looks like he can be Drake London for us. His ability to go get the ball is special, but he's more than that. I don't care what he runs in a 40. He's quicker than you think."

Boston has had a tremendous camp, so much so that head coach Todd Monken announced Boston will be moving into the starting lineup to play the "X" receiver with a plan to move around the formation with veteran Jerry Jeudy, who is having uneven training camp. Monken also said Boston's catch radius is an aspect he shares similarities with Mike Evans.

The transition paves the way for Boston to eventually become the Browns' No. 1 receiver. When I watched practice last week, Boston took over with catches on all three levels from both Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson. The trust was there. The QB situation is troubling for fantasy prospects, but if you were to make any upside play in this receiver room it feels like it's Boston.

First-round rookie KC Concepcion has flashed strong play in camp as well and should have a notable role, but the 6-foot-4 Boston already looks like a draft steal and could become the go-to receiver for a Browns team that has had notable early struggles offensively in training camp.

stories.headline: AFL overreactions: GOTY and MOTY should include finals
stories.summary: Errol Gulden scored arguably the most impressive goal of the season on Saturday, but it won't be considered for the Goal of the Year. Should it? It's time to react to the big topic of the week.
stories.body:
There are plenty of talking points after the AFL's qualifying and elimination finals, with one of the biggest being whether the goal and mark of the year awards should extend through the finals series.

Let's get to this week's overreactions column, where we judge the biggest takeaways as legitimate or irrational.

The GOTY and MOTY awards should include finals
Both Errol Gulden and Izak Rankine booted spectacular goals in their side's respective finals wins this past weekend. Both players demonstrated ridiculous individual skill and neither major would look out of place if it were declared the 2026 Goal of the Year winner. But, of course, under current AFL award criteria, finals games are excluded from both the goal and mark of the year awards. So that won't be happening.

Verdict: Not an overreaction

Let's start with the most pressing question. Why must the goal or mark of the year only come from a home and away season game? Why can't it come in a final? Is it to protect fairness, given with finals not every team plays the same number of games. Is it because the league wants to present the winners on Brownlow Medal night, which is staged during the finals series. Who knows?

What we do know is that the whole point of these awards is to crown the BEST mark and goal of the YEAR. Excluding any games from eligibility immediately contradicts what these awards are supposedly in place for.

If anything, shouldn't a brilliant goal or mark in finals football should count for more than the exact same during the home and away season? The stakes are higher in finals. The pressure is ratcheted up in finals. And there are more eyes on these games. This is one of the many factors why I believe Gulden's incredible goal late in the third quarter against the Lions on Saturday afternoon was the best goal of the entire year. For him to be in eligible because it came in a final is ridiculous.

Gulden wouldn't be the first Swan to be stiffed by this rule. Two years ago, also in a qualifying final at the SCG, Isaac Heeney took an absolute screamer over GWS defender Jack Buckley. It was comfortably the best mark of the year and yet it was ineligible to win the award. Go figure.

The AFL needs to sort this out immediately.

-- Jake Michaels

stories.headline: U.S. closes pool play with 105-64 rout of Czechia
stories.summary: The United States routed Czechia 105-64 to close out pool play at the FIBA World Cup and rebound from a tough performance against Italy.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier set the tone early to help the U.S. bounce back from its worst offensive performance in 50 years.

Stewart had 11 of her 19 points in the first quarter and Collier scored seven of her 12 in the second as the Americans routed Czechia 105-64 on Monday.

"I just wanted to be better. I just wanted to really lead by example," Stewart said. "Not only just from stats, but just the way that I was communicating to my teammates. This is a big moment for all of us and we need to take full advantage of it."

Stewart was coming off the worst shooting game in her stellar career for USA Basketball. She missed her first eight shots against Italy on Sunday before hitting the go-ahead basket in the 55-52 gritty win.

She got going early against the Czechs and finished 8-of-11 from the field to go along with seven rebounds and six assists while playing only 17 minutes.

"I knew the ball had to go in the basket for me, like come on," Stewart said with a smile. "I was trying to get out early, rebound and run and put pressure on the rim. I thought that overall as a team, we did a really good job of seeing the lanes that we weren't running last night and running them today."

The Americans won their 33rd in a row in the tournament, going back to a semifinal loss to Russia in the 2006 World Cup.

Next up for the U.S. is the quarterfinal round on Thursday. The Americans will face the winner of the Hungary vs. Japan game that takes place Tuesday.

Stewart had 11 points in the first 10 minutes as the U.S. jumped out to a 29-15 lead. The Americans had only 30 points in the first half against Italy. They kept it going in the second quarter behind Collier.

"We weren't happy with our performance yesterday, really on either side," Collier said. "So just coming with the mindset that we're going to play as hard as we can, we're going to be aggressive."

U.S. coach Kara Lawson said she just needed to remind her two veterans how good they are between the two games.

"They're both complete players and there's no doubt when they're playing at a really high level our team clicks, and so it was great to see them both come out with great aggression, with great confidence. Confident in who they are and what we were doing."

The Americans extended the advantage to 57-33 at the half. They weren't challenged in the second half by the Czechs as the lead ballooned to more than 40 points.

Stewart finished short of her World Cup career high of 23 points set against China in 2018.

Czechia finished winless in pool play. The Czechs were playing in their first World Cup since 2014. They won the silver medal when they hosted the event in 2010.

In other games Monday, China beat Italy; Germany topped Mali; Belgium beat Australia; Puerto Rico edged Turkey; France routed Nigeria; Spain beat Japan; and Hungary slipped past Korea.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.headline: Isack Hadjar to miss F1 Spanish GP as Liam Lawson continues at Red Bull
stories.summary: Liam Lawson will continue to deputize for Red Bull's injured Isak Hadjar at the first ever Madrid Grand Prix, the team confirmed Monday.
stories.body:
Liam Lawson will continue to deputize for Red Bull's injured Isack Hadjar at the first ever Madrid Grand Prix, the team confirmed Monday.

Lawson had stepped up from junior team Racing Bulls at the Dutch and Italian GPs after Hadjar suffered a wrist injury during a training session in August.

He will do so again for a third consecutive weekend for a race at the all-new Madring circuit.

As was the case at the last two races, Yuki Tsunoda will continue to deputize at Racing Bulls in Lawson's place.

Red Bull said that although Hadjar has continued to "progress positively" in his rehab, he is not yet ready to return.

Lawson's appearance in Hadjar's place at Monza had made it likely he would stay in the seat for this weekend's race given the tight turnaround between events.

Red Bull has not given a timeline on when they expect to have Hadjar back in the car.

After Madrid, F1 will race at Baku's Azerbaijan Grand Prix on Sep. 26.

stories.headline: Pochettino cautious about young stars for USMNT camp amid buzz around Sullivan, Hall
stories.summary: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and NYRB's Julian Hall.
stories.body:
United States men's national team coach Mauricio Pochettino said that while he is happy about the potential of young players in the U.S. pool, "we need to be careful" amid the buzz around Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan and Red Bull New York's Julian Hall.

The U.S. has scheduled a quartet of friendlies starting at the end of the month, starting with a match against Peru on Sept. 26, Chile on Sept. 29, Mexico on Oct. 3, and then Canada on Oct. 6. The roster will be announced on Sept. 17, with players beginning to arrive in Atlanta three days later.

As such there is much anticipation about what young players might get called up, including Sullivan and Hall.

Upon signing on for another World Cup cycle last month, Pochettino said he would be "starting from zero" in terms of building his team.

Speaking to reporters via video conference from London, Pochettino stressed he is trying to look at the potential of young players in a balanced way, and not let expectations get ahead of a player's development.

"I think we are very happy about to have all these potential good players being young, and with a possibility to perform and to play," Pochettino said.

"Only we need to be careful. We need to be careful because when you are young, of course you need to be confident, you need to have the trust in yourself, and believe that you can perform and you can do well. But the thing is it's a limit. The balance is the most important.

"And one of our responsibilities is to protect this guy because sometime if you play well and you are 17, 16 or 18 and you play well and people started to know to talk about that you are Messi or you are a big star in the world because you do some few good things. If after you are confused and you don't manage well, that can be dangerous for your career.

"And that is what we don't want. [We want] the young guys with potential being top players to provide the platform for them to evolve and to be professional, to build their career in the best way, improving every day, being humble, being careful when they talk in the media, when they talk with the teammate, when they talk with the opponent. I think respect is the most important thing and they need to be respectful. And of course we want players with talent."

Pochettino said that one goal for this cycle to further eradicate some bad habits that currently exist in the program.

Part of this the alignment of youth and professional clubs with the U.S. Soccer Federation.

The USSF recently announced a takeover of U.S. Youth Soccer.

"I think it's important when we talk about habits, it's about talking about everything, because after the player behave on the field because of this type of decision, they came from the top, he said.

"And we need to be aligned all together in our principles and all the concept that we need to improve if we want to be competitive in every single moment in our [path] until to the first team. I think we are all focused in trying to add our knowledge."

But Pochettino added that the bad habits also include players deciding not to take part competitive tournaments like the Gold Cup.

This a reference to players like Christian Pulisic who opted to sit out the 2025 Gold Cup in order to recover from a long club season.

"We were talking [about] the habit. Before it was difficult to make the roster for the World Cup one year before, because the mindset was different and say, 'Oh, if I play, I have not holidays, I cannot arrive fresh for the World Cup," Pochettino said.

"Already, with the time, you know now that is bulls--- -- sorry -- and I think it's to change this type of idea that are not right and that our experience to build mindset with the coaches, with the people in the organization, in the clubs, and of course us, and then the player that in the way that we will plan and we will do the things is the best for them, for the player, and it's going to be the best for soccer in the USA."

Pochettino added that despite the USMNT playing four games during the window, he will bring in his standard number of 26 players, including four goalkeepers.

Anything more than that would mean some players wouldn't get minutes.

"In this period of the season, we need to be careful with the player that we are going to call," he said.

"We need the players that we'll call that [they] be available to train, but also to play. And I think we consider it at the moment ,and to call 26 players with four keepers. And I think more than this is I think it's an issue because after to train, to share the minutes, I think the player that we are going to have, we want to see, we want to give the possibility to play ... with the possibility to compete. That is the idea for the next camp."

Pochettino indicated that some players who have just switched clubs, like the Middlesbrough duo of defender Max Arfsten and midfielder Sebastian Berhalter, might not be called in in order to give them more time to settle into their new surroundings.

But he indicated there would be a balance between youth and experience.

"I think we cannot bring the whole squad [with] young players because they need to have some guys with experience already competing," Pochettino said.

"But yes, we are going to do a mix ... I think experienced player with young player that can fit together and start to work on how the young kid start to manage the pressure to play in the first team."

stories.headline: NBA offseason recap, early 2026-27 season previews by team
stories.summary: We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the regular season by rolling out one team profile each weekday through Sept. 18.
stories.body:
After an eventful July full of big trades, intriguing signings and the game's biggest star shocking everyone by heading East, the NBA offseason is nearly complete. And with the regular-season schedule now out, it's time to start thinking about the 2026-27 season.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for every team.

Check out the rollout schedule below, with stories added daily:

Quick links:

Free agency buzz | FA grades | Trade grades

Transactions | Schedule | More NBA coverage

Central Division

Milwaukee Bucks: Sept. 7
Key additions: Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Caris LeVert

Key retentions: Gary Trent Jr.

Key subtractions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis

After 13 seasons, the Giannis era ended in Milwaukee with a mega trade to the Heat -- and the 2026-27 season will mark a major shift for the rebuilding franchise.

The Bucks hired coach Taylor Jenkins to establish a culture. They added four new players from Miami, including former All-Star and Wisconsin native Tyler Herro, and selected Brayden Burries with the No. 10 pick in June.

The Bucks will enter the season with an ill-fitting mix of players and low expectations, but they have the luxury to see what sticks long term. -- Jamal Collier

Read the full Bucks offseason recap/season preview

Chicago Bulls: Sept. 8

Cleveland Cavaliers: Sept. 9

Indiana Pacers: Sept. 10

Detroit Pistons: Sept. 11

Southeast Division

Miami Heat: Aug. 31
Key additions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson, Bobby Portis, Tim Hardaway Jr., Nick Richards

Key retentions: Andrew Wiggins, Simone Fontecchio

Key subtractions: Tyler Herro, Norman Powell, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis

Heat president Pat Riley landed the superstar he'd been searching for since LeBron James left Miami in 2016. Antetokounmpo is in the fold, and Miami is ready to contend for another title with the two-time MVP. Antetokounmpo is just as motivated to win his second title and remind everyone that he can be the best player in the league.

In the trade, the Heat gave up key players such as Herro, Ware and Jaquez and did not bring back Powell in free agency. They landed Thompson to a two-year, $13 million deal after the four-time champion sharpshooter worked out a buyout with the Dallas Mavericks. Miami also added Portis and Hardaway, but the team is still looking to bolster the roster around Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Heat offseason recap/season preview

Washington Wizards: Sept. 1
Key additions: AJ Dybantsa, Khris Middleton, Deandre Ayton, Tre Mann

Key subtractions: Cam Whitmore, D'Angelo Russell, Jaden Hardy

Key retentions: Trae Young

The Wizards got their jump on this pivotal offseason by acquiring Trae Young and Anthony Davis last season in trades.

Those were their two big moves and then came the big prize for losing 65 games last season - winning the lottery and drafting AJ Dybantsa with the first overall pick.

Ready to start winning games this season after losing 60 or more games in each of the past three years, Washington gave Young a four-year, $212 million contract. The Wizards added veterans like Khris Middleton and Deandre Ayton to bolster the depth behind their young core featuring the likes of Dybantsa, Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George, Tre Johnson and Will Riley. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Wizards offseason recap/season preview

Charlotte Hornets: Sept. 2
Key additions: F Naz Reid, G Grayson Allen, G Dennis Schroder, F Royce O'Neale, F Dorian Finney-Smith

Key retentions: G Coby White

Key subtractions: G LaMelo Ball, F Miles Bridges, G Josh Green, G Tre Mann

After enjoying their best season in a decade, the Hornets sharply changed course with the surprising decision to trade Ball, their franchise guard, to the Timberwolves.

Given that Ball was a borderline All-Star on a max contract, Charlotte opted for a "Moneyball" approach in hopes of avoiding the perpetual mediocrity that tripped up Trae Young's Atlanta Hawks in the recent past.

With Ball and starting forward Miles Bridges moved in separate deals aimed at collecting future draft assets and improving its cap flexibility, Charlotte is now the only team that doesn't have a single player on the books for at least $25 million next season. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Hornets offseason recap/season preview

Atlanta Hawks: Sept. 3
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason.

The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall.

Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Hawks offseason recap/season preview

Orlando Magic: Sept. 4
Key additions: C Nikola Vucevic, G Izaiyah Nelson

Key subtractions: F Moritz Wagner, G Jett Howard

Key retentions: F Jonathan Isaac, G Jevon Carter

The Magic's biggest move this offseason was hiring Sean Sweeney to replace Jamahl Mosley.

Orlando also brought Nikola Vucevic back on a one-year, $3.9 million deal since trading him in 2021 and will use his ability to score and shoot to space the floor for Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Desmond Bane.

The Magic blew a 3-1 lead over top-seeded Detroit in the first round of the playoffs after Wagner went down due to injury and were in desperate need of someone who can get easier baskets and make outside shots. Vucevic should help. Moe Wagner departed for Brooklyn via free agency, separating Franz from his brother for the first time in his pro career. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Read the full Magic offseason recap/season preview

Pacific Division

Los Angeles Lakers: Aug. 24
Key additions: C Walker Kessler, F Sandro Mamukelashvili, G Quentin Grimes, G Collin Sexton, F Kevon Looney, F Matisse Thybulle, G Cameron Carr

Key retentions: G Austin Reaves

Key subtractions: F LeBron James, C Deandre Ayton, G Marcus Smart, F Rui Hachimura, G Luke Kennard, C Jaxson Hayes

James informed the Lakers he would not be returning for next season on June 30. Two days later, the team transformed the roster, with Doncic squarely as the focal point.

The biggest addition -- literally and figuratively -- is 7-foot-2 center Kessler, acquired in a sign-and-trade deal with the Utah Jazz. L.A. sent two unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and pick swaps in 2028 and 2030, not to mention a four-year, $130 million contract, to acquire him.

Mamukelashvili, Grimes, Sexton, Looney and Thybulle also signed with the Lakers, and free agent Ziaire Williams and first-round pick Carr bolster the team's young prospect pool of Adou Thiero, Bronny James and Dalton Knecht.

The most important move, though, came when Reaves, coming off a career season in which he averaged 23.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 5.5 assists per game, signed a four-year, $180 million extension.

When the dust settled, it was a dramatic roster overhaul in what could prove to be one of the most consequential summers in franchise history, with the team also being sold for the second time in 14 months, this time to venture capitalist Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger, who bought the Lakers from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Lakers offseason recap/season preview

LA Clippers: Aug. 25
Key additions: Rui Hachimura, Keaton Wagler, Brandon Ingram (TBD), Gradey Dick (TBD)

Key retentions: Kobe Sanders, Bradley Beal

Key subtractions: Kawhi Leonard (TBD), Nicolas Batum, Bogdan Bogdanovic, John Collins

What started as a reconfiguration at the trade deadline -- acquiring Darius Garland from Cleveland for James Harden and Bennedict Mathurin from Indiana for Ivica Zubac -- turned into a complete overhaul this summer after the Clippers let Bogdan Bogdanovic, Nicolas Batum and John Collins walk.

Their biggest move, however, was trading Leonard to the Toronto Raptors for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks, but that deal is in limbo pending the investigation into alleged salary cap circumvention by the team relating to Leonard's Aspiration endorsement deal.

In the meantime, LA added Illinois guard Wagler with the No. 5 pick in the draft and signed Hachimura away from the crosstown Lakers with a two-year, $28 million deal. And in a surprise move, Bradley Beal -- after declining his $5.6 million contract option for next season in June to test free agency -- ended up re-signing on a two-year, $13.2 million deal in mid-August to stay with the Clippers. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Clippers offseason recap/season preview

Golden State Warriors: Aug. 26
Key additions: Yaxel Lendeborg, Brandon Williams, Georges Niang

Key subtractions: Quinten Post, Pat Spencer

Key retentions: Draymond Green, Al Horford, Kristaps Porzingis, Gary Payton II, De'Anthony Melton

The Warriors opted for flexibility and stability over a larger shake-up around Curry. Their much-publicized recruitment of James never gained much traction.

They brought back their veteran frontcourt trio (Green, Horford, Porzingis), but kept them all on short-term maneuverable contracts. They opted for the fit of Melton over a pursuit of scoring guard Anfernee Simons. Their big addition is Lendeborg, the 23-year-old rookie wing who they will rely upon to be a high-minute, high-impact rotation player immediately.

In the bigger picture, they protected their draft pick cupboard and lined up their books to have an ocean of cap space as they peer a bit deeper into the future while their core ages. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Warriors offseason recap/season preview

Phoenix Suns: Aug. 27
Key additions: F Miles Bridges, F Koa Peat, G Luke Kennard

Key subtractions: G Grayson Allen, F Royce O'Neale

Key retentions: F Dillon Brooks, G Collin Gillespie, C Mark Williams, G Jordan Goodwin

Phoenix followed up its surprising season with a series of moves to mostly keep its team intact, with some adjustments around the margins.

The Suns re-signed Gillespie (four years, $48 million), Williams (three years, $38 million), Goodwin (three years, $19 million) and Brooks (three years, $73 million) to new deals and made a major splash by trading Allen and O'Neale to the Charlotte Hornets for Bridges. And despite not having a pick until No. 47 in the second round of the 2026 draft, Phoenix was able to acquire Arizona player Peat -- who averaged 14.1 points on 52.8% shooting as a freshman for the Wildcats and was key to their Final Four run. -- Dave McMenamin

Read the full Suns offseason recap/season preview

Sacramento Kings: Aug. 28
Key additions: G Darius Acuff Jr., F Alex Karaban, G Emanuel Sharp

Key subtractions: G DeMar DeRozan, G Russell Westbrook

Key retentions: F Precious Achiuwa

Perry, currently in the organization's power seat, is continuing a steady transition toward the younger core he has drafted. Arkansas guard and No. 7 pick Acuff is the spotlight name on a roster populated with six players in their first two NBA seasons.

But they still have notable high-minute holdovers from the past regime, including Murray, Malik Monk, LaVine and Sabonis. Of those four, Murray appears the most locked-in as a stable member of the team's long-term vision. Perry explored trades for Monk, LaVine and Sabonis over the past year, but didn't value the proposed returns, and the three are expected to open the season in Sacramento. -- Anthony Slater

Read the full Kings offseason recap/season preview

Northwest Division

Portland Trail Blazers: Aug. 17
Key additions: G Ja Morant, F Jeremy Sochan

Key retentions: C Robert Williams III

Key subtractions: F Jerami Grant, F Kris Murray, G Matisse Thybulle

Sadly, the Blazers made far more noise this offseason with their off-court business dealings than anything they did with their roster. New owner Tom Dundon's aggressive cost-cutting measures and ongoing fight for arena financing have distracted from the progress that Portland made on the court last season, when it reached the playoffs for the first time since 2021.

Although the Blazers were the only team that sat out June's draft by not making a pick, they will add two high-profile guards to a rotation that otherwise looks very similar to last season. Lillard, a franchise icon, is back from an Achilles tendon injury that sidelined him for the entire 2025-26 campaign, and Morant, a two-time All-Star, arrived in a trade that sent Grant and Murray to the Memphis Grizzlies. -- Ben Golliver

Read the full Blazers offseason recap/season preview

Utah Jazz: Aug. 18
Key additions: G Darryn Peterson, C Jaxson Hayes, G Josh Okogie

Key retentions: C Jusuf Nurkic

Key subtractions: C Walker Kessler

The Jazz finally got some lottery luck, landing at No. 2 and taking Peterson, a gifted guard who has the potential to emerge as the face of the franchise. The hope was that Peterson would be the final major piece in Utah's rebuild, but that plan featured Kessler as the team's long-term starting center. Instead, the Jazz agreed to a sign-and-trade deal that sent Kessler to the Lakers in exchange for a pair of future first-round picks and two swaps.

The return was widely considered to be great value for Utah, particularly after Kessler's deal (four years, $130 million) pushed beyond the Jazz's comfort zone, but there is now a glaring need in the starting lineup alongside Jackson and Lauri Markkanen in the frontcourt. -- Tim MacMahon

Read the full Jazz offseason recap/season preview

Minnesota Timberwolves: Aug. 19
Key additions: G LaMelo Ball, G Josh Green, G Isaiah Evans

Key subtractions: F Julius Randle, C Naz Reid

Key retentions: G Ayo Dosunmu, G Bones Hyland, G Jaylen Clark

Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly continued to show his aggression, orchestrating a four-team trade with the Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets that sent out three-time All-Star Randle and the 2023-24 Sixth Man of the Year, Reid, and a future first-round pick to bring in the talented -- but polarizing -- Ball.

That move followed Connelly inking 6-foot-4 guard Dosunmu to a five-year, $112 million extension in June, following his acquisition at the deadline.

Minnesota also re-signed wing Clark and guard Hyland and acquired the 6-foot-6 Evans out of Duke with the No. 33 pick in the draft.

Coach Chris Finch also lost his top lieutenant on the bench, Micah Nori, who left to coach the Portland Trail Blazers. -- Dave McMenamin

They sent Isaiah Joe to Detroit and traded Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort to Atlanta in separate moves, eroding their depth.

General manager Sam Presti made clear in an interview with The Oklahoman that the impression he's been given from ownership is "the savings generated this summer, and from being out of the tax the last several years, will be re-allocated to future teams."

That would mean extra breathing room to eventually extend core young players such as Cason Wallace and Ajay Mitchell. Wallace, the likely replacement starter for Dort, is extension eligible off his rookie contract into October. -- Anthony Slater

But retaining the 23-year-old would have been expensive -- via either a sky-high luxury tax bill or a salary-slashing move to get off an important veteran and generate more breathing room for a new deal.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey forward tiers: Who to draft and when to take them
stories.summary: Use these forward tiers to help you plan out your fantasy hockey draft strategy.
stories.body:
Picture the boarding line at the airport.

They call Group 1, and here's the thing about Group 1, it does not matter one bit where in that group you're standing. First person or last, you're strolling on with your bag and your pick of the overhead bin. Everyone in the group is, functionally, the same.

Then they call Group 2 ... still totally fine, still getting your bag up top. Group 3, you're eyeing the bins nervously, but at least you're all in the same boat. Er, plane.

By the time they're calling Group 6, you're handing your carry-on to the gate agent and hoping to see it in the next time zone -- but so is everyone else in your group.

That drop, from group to group, real and steep, with near-total equality inside each group? That's a tier list. That's the whole idea. And that's how you should draft.

Here's why it saves you at a draft. Say you've got your eye on one guy, and the two picks ahead of you snap him and the player right next to him up. On a flat ranking, you panic. Scramble down to whatever's left with the clock screaming at you. But if you already knew those two were sitting in the same boarding group as three other players you rated just as highly? You don't flinch. You wave the next one aboard and you've lost nothing.

That's the magic -- you stop making 150 individual decisions and start making a handful of "anyone in this group is fine" ones. It's the same reason you don't need to stampede toward the jetway when your group is called. Everyone in it lands in the same place.

The fantasy forward groups below are mine. My projections, my drop-offs, my problem when I'm wrong. They aren't the official in-game ranks you'll see inside the ESPN Fantasy Hockey.

These come from my own projections: a base of each player's three-year average, a sprinkle of how comparable players the same age have fared across the past 15 seasons, and a dash of manual adjustment for the spots where my gut overrules the math. The projected ESPN standard points sit right next to each name below, so you can see exactly where I've got everyone slotted.

Note: Points based on the ESPN standard scoring system.
