stories.headline: A bit 'unfair': Sharks players unhappy over finals call
stories.summary: Cronulla firebrand Addin Fonua-Blake says it's unfair that Saturday night's home final cannot be played at Shark Park, despite Peter V'landys' insistence the decision has the support of a lot of the club's fans.
stories.body:
Cronulla firebrand Addin Fonua-Blake says it's unfair that Saturday night's home final cannot be played at Shark Park, despite Peter V'landys' insistence the decision has the support of a lot of the club's fans.

The Sharks received a massive personnel boost on Monday, with Braydon Trindall training and Fonua-Blake revealing he expected the star five-eighth to play.

But Cronulla players were also left to admit their disappointment at not being allowed to face North Queensland at Shark Park, with the game instead set for Allianz Stadium.

The NRL's decision comes after years of debate around finals venues, with Shark Park the most scrutinised given its currently-reduced capacity of 13,500 amid an ongoing leagues' club reconstruction.

Cronulla bosses had been hopeful the fact the club were playing the Cowboys would allow the game to be played at a suburban ground, given the likelihood of fewer away fans.

But that hope was officially snuffed on Sunday, raising questions over whether Shark Park would ever host a finals match again.

"It's not ideal," Fonua-Blake said.

"You work so hard during the year to get a home semi and for it to be taken away, it's unfair.

"It's the incentive for finishing higher on the ladder, and to not get it, it's a bit unfair."

The NSW State of Origin prop said his concern was driven by the fact most clubs could play at their home stadium.

"To play in front of your home crowd, it feels like you have a 14th player on the field sometimes," he said.

"It's a bit unfair, but what can you do? The call has been made above our heads.

"We've just got to cop it and get ready to go out and put in a good performance this weekend."

The NRL changed its rules at the end of last season to give it the ultimate say on where finals would be played.

But Australian Rugby League Commission chairman V'landys insisted on Monday that the door was not forever shut on all suburban grounds hosting finals in the future.

"We're going to look at every game on its merits," said V'landys, who is also currently acting as NRL executive chairman.

"We still want to try to keep the suburban grounds as much as possible.

"But when their capacity and their facilities aren't there at the standard you want, you've got to shift them.

"Unfortunately, at the moment, Shark Park, I don't think anyone can argue, isn't that facility where you're giving the fan the ultimate experience."

When asked how Cronulla took the news, V'landys said it had been made with the club's fans in mind.

"A lot of Sharks fans wanted to go to Allianz, believe it or not," he said.

"And we wanted to accommodate them. Plus, we wanted to accommodate a lot more fans.

"Why would you have a billion-dollar venue sitting there doing nothing? Why not give fans the ultimate comfort and the ultimate experience?"

stories.headline: Giants release WR Darius Slayton, team's longest-tenured player
stories.summary: The Giants have released wide receiver Darius Slayton, moving on from their longest-tenured player.
stories.body:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants on Monday released wide receiver Darius Slayton, the longest-tenured player on the team.

Slayton was a fifth-round draft pick of the Giants in 2018, the same year they took Daniel Jones with the No. 6 selection. Slayton had 296 catches for 4,435 yards receiving yards and 22 touchdowns in seven seasons in New York.

The Giants signed Slayton to a three-year, $36 million deal before last season. He was due $13 million this season.

The move creates just over $3 million in cap space for this year.

"Grateful for my time in NY. 7 years a Giant nothing but love for one of the most prestigious organizations in the NFL. Excited to see what's next," he posted to X on Monday.

Slayton, 29, had six seasons of at least 500 yards receiving for the Giants. But he found himself out of favor with new coach John Harbaugh this summer after undergoing core muscle surgery in the spring. Slayton started the summer strong but never seemed to quite get his footing in the new offense with a new coaching staff.

The writing was on the wall when the Giants signed wide receiver Darnell Mooney in free agency. They later added Odell Beckham Jr. in the spring.

Harbaugh has said the intention is for Beckham to play. He will be part of the "rotation" and in sub packages. With Malik Nabers eyeing a Week 1 return from his knee injury suffered last season, rookie Malachi Fields impressing and Mooney and Beckham ahead of him on the depth chart, Slayton was left in limbo over the past week.

New York was open to moving him during final cuts, sources told ESPN. The significant salary made a trade difficult.

"You kind of just figure out the league the more you're around," Slayton said last week. "At the end of the day, you control what you can control and let the rest fall where it may."

Slayton is now a free agent. He's not eligible for waivers as a vested veteran and is free to sign elsewhere.

Slayton's career with the Giants had its fair share of ups and downs. He struggled catching the ball during rookie minicamp but quickly found his way onto the field. The Auburn product had 740 yards and a career-best eight touchdowns his rookie season.

But Slayton later found himself buried on the depth chart when coach Brian Daboll and general manager Joe Schoen took over in 2022. Slayton still eventually worked his way back into the rotation and again became the team's leading receiver that year.

He was the Giants' leading receiver on four occasions (2019, 2020, 2022 and 2023). But he also struggled with drops and inconsistencies, making him a constant target for fans' disgust.

Slayton has 26 drops since entering the league in 2019, tied for 12th most among wide receivers.

stories.headline: Sky owner calls Kanter Freedom's free speech lawsuit 'meritless'
stories.summary: Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter called a lawsuit filed by Enes Kanter Freedom "meritless and frivolous."
stories.body:
Chicago Sky owner Michael Alter called a lawsuit filed by Enes Kanter Freedom "meritless and frivolous" Friday afternoon.

Kanter Freedom alleged that his First Amendment rights were violated when he was removed from a Sky home game Aug. 23 and then banned from attending Sky games at the arena. The former NBA player was removed from the building after getting in a verbal altercation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter against the Indiana Fever. He was sitting courtside in a black T-shirt that read: "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

Kanter Freedom put up his arms and began to walk toward the court from his baseline seat as he and Cloud exchanged words. He stepped past media camera operators to approach the floor; security stopped him and subsequently ejected him. Alter had previously explained that Kanter Freedom made himself "the potential to be a threat" by stepping toward the court and players.

A 15-page complaint was filed Thursday in the Northern District of Illinois Eastern Division and listed the defendants as the Sky, the city of Chicago, and Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority, which owns and operates Wintrust Arena.

"This lawsuit is meritless and frivolous," Alter said in a statement Friday. "Freedom's claim that he was removed from Wintrust Arena due to his speech is false. As his own complaint acknowledges, he wore the shirt in question for multiple hours without any contact with security. Security removed Freedom only after he violated fan code of conduct by rising from his seat, gesturing at a player, and stepping toward the court.

"Freedom was removed for his conduct, not his speech. We look forward to the truth prevailing in court."

Kanter Freedom has inserted himself in the political realm in recent years and has been vocal in the national debate sparked by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's comments regarding transgender athletes. He and former NBA player Royce White recently declared themselves women and eligible to play in the WNBA. They are not eligible to play in the league, multiple sources told ESPN.

On social media, Kanter Freedom posted that he was "peacefully exercising" his First Amendment rights.

"My T-shirt did what the whole WNBA apparently couldn't: define a woman," Kanter Freedom wrote. "No threats. No violence. Just biology. And somehow, that required a security escort.

"You don't have to agree with my speech but you don't get to silence me for it. I will not be intimidated. I will not be silenced. I will continue to stand for women and defend free speech."

stories.headline: Arsenal's Ezri Konsa 'loved' battle with England teammate Morgan Rogers in Chelsea clash
stories.summary: Ezri Konsa was delighted with his tackle on former teammate Morgan Rogers that brought a roar of approval from Arsenal fans during Sunday's 2-1 win over Chelsea.
stories.body:
Ezri Konsa was delighted with his tackle on former Aston Villa teammate Morgan Rogers that brought a roar of approval from Arsenal fans during Sunday's 2-1 win over Chelsea.

The champions were defending a one-goal lead late in the match when Rogers threatened to go clean through on goal until he was stopped in his tracks by a perfectly-timed challenge from Konsa on his home debut.

The Emirates Stadium crowd reacted with a cheer almost as loud the one that greeted the winning goal scored by Martin Odegaard early in the second half, as Mikel Arteta's side recovered from a goal down to maintain their perfect start to the season.

"I love duels," Konsa said. "As a defender, I think these are things you have to cherish.

"For me personally, I love a challenge. I love being in duels. I had a few today and I'm glad I came out on top.

"[Rogers] is a good friend of mine, but on the pitch, it's a different story. I saw the opportunity to go in and make the tackle and it came off."

Arsenal fell behind to a volley from Rogers after 77 seconds but hit back to level midway through the first half, Kai Havertz cutting in off the flank to beat Emiliano Martínez and score against his former team.

Chelsea's front three of Cole Palmer, João Pedro and Rogers were lively again but the visitors ultimately could not find their way past Konsa and co for a second time.

"I really enjoyed the occasion," the England defender said. "My first London derby and I thought the fans were fantastic, superb. They stayed behind us throughout the whole game; without them, these games are impossible.

"Conceding so early isn't great, and I know we take a lot of pride here in keeping clean sheets, but I thought the reaction was second to none, it was fantastic. It just goes to show the character and the mentality of this team."

Konsa, who made his debut in last week's 1-0 win away against his former side Villa, was in the side on Sunday in place of Cristhian Mosquera, who was injured, and long-term absentee William Saliba.

Like I said before in previous interviews, this style really suits me -- I love the boss' way of playing. stories.headline: Ex-F1 chief Bernie Ecclestone stopped for illegally bringing shotgun to Portugal
stories.summary: Bernie Ecclestone said he was stopped by police at an airport in Portugal for bringing a shotgun into the country he intended to use in a clay pigeon shooting competition.
stories.body:
Bernie Ecclestone said he was stopped by police at an airport in Portugal for bringing a shotgun into the country he intended to use in a clay pigeon shooting competition.

The 95-year-old former Formula 1 boss told the Press Association that he had to "surrender" the weapon because he did not have the correct documents - but denied he was arrested.

The incident took place on Monday after Ecclestone landed in Cascais -- about 20 miles outside of Lisbon -- on a flight from Switzerland.

Ecclestone, who ruled F1 for four decades before he was deposed in 2017, said he spoke to customs officers and "four police" officers for "about an hour."

Explaining the events, Ecclestone told PA: "I was going to take part in Portugal in a clay pigeon shooting competition, which I only knew about a few days ago because Fabiana [his wife] met someone when she was coming back from Brazil to Portugal. He said he was entering into a clay pigeon competition.

"So she called me and said, 'There is something here you should go and look at. Why don't you turn up and join?' And I said, 'Well, that wouldn't be a bad idea'.

"As I have got guns already in Switzerland, which have been imported properly, because we do a bit of clay pigeon shooting there, I brought the gun in with me.

"I went through customs and the people know me very well. They said, 'Anything to declare?' I said, 'No, nothing really, just all the usual personal things.'

"So I walked out and, as I got out, one of my people with me said, 'The police have asked if you would go and see them'.

"I went to see the police and said, 'What can I do for you?' And they said, 'We would like some information on this gun you brought in.'

"I didn't even unzip the case. I said, 'Well, it is a shotgun and this is the reason.' And they asked where is the blue book for the gun?

And I said, 'I don't know, I have never heard about a blue book in my life.'

"They said, 'Yes, well anyone with these guns should always have the book, it is like a passport. Incidentally, I want to look at your passport, too,' which they took.

"I said, 'I bought the gun in England and took it into Switzerland through all the normal channels.' And they said, 'Where is the blue book?'

And I said, 'I just told you, I don't know about the blue book.'

"There were about four police guys and they said, 'What you have done is try to import a gun into the country.' I said, 'I have not tried to do that. I have come through customs, and here I am with you,' and they were like, 'It is a gun and we need all the particulars for the gun, and I can I have a look at your passport, and we need the blue book for the gun.'

"So all this nonsense went on. We went back to the customs, and the police had complained to customs, and the customs officer said, 'You need to surrender the gun here in Lisbon and then we will look at it there, and do you want to import it? And if so, you will have to pay duty on it and ask for a temporary import, and we will deal with it like that.' So I said, 'Well we'd better do that.'"

Responding to reports he had been arrested, Ecclestone replied: "No. The police were very helpful and doing all they could to stop us from having to do what we had to do."

Four years ago, Ecclestone had a handgun on him before he boarded a flight in Sao Paulo. He was stopped by police and had to pay 6,000 Brazilian reals (£1,000/$1,170), to the local authorities. The gun was confiscated.

stories.headline: MLS Power Rankings: Griezmann catapults Orlando into the playoff picture
stories.summary: With eight goal contributions in eight games since joining the Lions, Antoine Griezmann has turned around Orlando's season. That and more in ESPN's MLS Power Rankings.
stories.body:
It's Monday, another weekend of action is in the books, and it's time for the latest edition of ESPN's MLS Power Rankings.

1. Nashville SC
Previous ranking: 1

While Nashville dropped points in a 0-0 draw against New York City on Friday, their biggest competitors for the Supporters' Shield slipped up, too. Both Vancouver and Miami failed to win, leaving Nashville with a 10-point lead atop the Shield race.

2. Vancouver Whitecaps
Previous ranking: 2

Despite taking an early lead, the Whitecaps quickly crumbled in a 3-1 home defeat against St. Louis. In what was, perhaps, their worst match of the season, Vancouver fell apart before halftime en route to losing to fellow contender out West for the second time in four games.

3. St. Louis City SC
Previous ranking: 7

You couldn't have written a better script for St. Louis' Saturday night. Not only did new additions Rafael Navarro and Damion Downs make their debuts in the second half, but the visitors took the game to Vancouver and secured a 3-1 road victory. Doubt St. Louis' contender status at your own peril.

4. Inter Miami CF
Previous ranking: 3

Miami's Achilles heel is widely known: they're a team that gets easily scrambled in their own third. With two sloppy fouls conceding two penalties to Atlanta, Saturday's 2-2 draw with the Five Stripes was the latest example of Inter Miami's defensive play letting them down.

5. LAFC
Previous ranking: 5

Despite holding a one-goal lead heading into the intermission, LAFC's second-half concession saw them earn just a point on the road against Salt Lake. An unwillingness -- or inability -- to keep the ball late in games continues to bite for the Black & Gold.

6. FC Cincinnati
Previous ranking: 6

After their scheduled meeting with D.C. United was postponed due to inclement weather, Cincinnati will have extra time to bed in their defensive reinforcements. That 4-0 loss to Nashville last time out still stings.

7. Chicago Fire
Previous ranking: 4

The good news? Chicago bagged four goals on Saturday, including one from Robert Lewandowski as he continues to find his place in the attack. The bad news? Chicago conceded four in a 4-4 draw with Toronto. It's safe to say Chicago are missing rising star Mbekezeli Mbokazi in the backline.

8. New York City FC
Previous ranking: 9

Up against a fearsome Nashville team, New York City manager Pascal Jansen opted for a fairly conservative approach on Friday. Ceding most of the ball, the Pigeons did well to keep Nashville scoreless, but they failed to create much danger themselves in a 0-0 home draw.

9. New England Revolution
Previous ranking: 8

Trailing by two goals at halftime, the Revs couldn't find a way to equalize against the Galaxy on their way to a 2-1 road defeat. While Carles Gil's penalty conversion got them on the board, questions remain about whether the options New England have placed around him will produce.

10. Houston Dynamo
Previous ranking: 10

Despite having a man advantage for the final 20-plus minutes of the match, Houston had a hard time creating much of anything in their 0-0 road draw with Charlotte. While attacking questions remain for Ben Olsen's outfit, the Dynamo's string of shutdown defensive showings mark them as a team that must be taken seriously.

11. Charlotte FC
Previous ranking: 13

While Charlotte couldn't find a breakthrough during their 0-0 home draw with Houston, Allan Saint-Maximin looked like the best player on the field. Dean Smith's new left winger was at the center of nearly every threatening move and has the look of an MLS star.

12. Real Salt Lake
Previous ranking: 12

Still winless in league play since May, RSL drew 2-2 with LAFC on Saturday. They created a slew of quality chances, but also proved too open in defensive transition as control and tactical balance still eludes them.

13. Orlando City
Previous ranking: 16

Antoine Griezmann continued his absolute tear with the lone goal in Orlando's 1-0 win over San Diego. Now with eight goal contributions in eight games since debuting for the Lions, Griezmann has quickly turned around Orlando's season: they're now above the playoff line in the East.

14. FC Dallas
Previous ranking: 14

If there's a debate about MLS's best striker, Petar Musa is doing his best to end it. The Croatia international managed two goals, including the game winner, and an assist in Dallas' 4-3 win over Kansas City. While the home side's focus lacked, Musa's certainly didn't.

15. Philadelphia Union
Previous ranking: 15

Since league play resumed after the World Cup, the Union are yet to lose. Saturday's 2-0 victory over Montréal lengthened that streak of results to eight games, with six of them going down as wins. With yet another goal from Cavan Sullivan, Philadelphia are flying.

16. San Diego FC
Previous ranking: 15

Missing star midfielder Jeppe Tverskov due to a card suspension, San Diego's ball progression never turned into regular chances in a 1-0 road loss to Orlando. Without the Dane, the sophomore side simply can't carry the same threat going forward.

17. Minnesota United
Previous ranking: 11

For a team that prides itself on effective defending, conceding three goals in the first half in a 5-4 loss to the Timbers was nowhere near good enough for Minnesota. Still, breakout striker Marcus Caldeira's brace could signal longer-term attacking improvement for a team fighting for a playoff spot.

18. LA Galaxy
Previous ranking: 20

The Galaxy marked Sergi Roberto's first MLS start with a 2-1 victory over New England. The former Barcelona man was a touch magnet in central midfield, helping his new team conduct play. If Roberto and Chucky Lozano, who notched an assist, maintain this form, the Galaxy won't be easily dismissed.

19. Toronto FC
Previous ranking: 22

Josh Sargent appears to be finding his form in MLS. While the U.S. striker had a quiet start to life in Toronto, he notched a hat trick in a 4-4 draw with Chicago over the weekend. It was a top-tier showing from Sargent atop Robin Fraser's attacking structure that led to a point for the hosts.

20. Red Bull New York
Previous ranking: 19

Now below the playoff line out East following a 0-0 draw in Seattle, that Red Bull New York didn't do more in the summer transfer window is a major concern. Without any game-changing additions made to the squad before deadline day, it's difficult to see how Michael Bradley's team will rebound.

21. Seattle Sounders
Previous ranking: 21

On Saturday, Sounders fans could breathe a collective sigh of relief upon seeing Cristian Roldan make his first start for the team since May. Still, the USMNT midfielder's return wasn't enough to see Seattle claim their first win in months. A 0-0 draw with the Red Bulls had to suffice.

22. Portland Timbers
Previous ranking: 23

With star striker Kevin Kelsy now off to Rangers in the Scottish Premiership, replacement Vincent Janssen didn't waste any time filling the Venezuelan's shoes. Janssen notched a hat trick in the Timbers' wild 5-4 home win over Minnesota.

23. San Jose Earthquakes
Previous ranking: 18

It looked as if the Quakes' winless run, one that stretches all the way back to May, was going to come to an end on Saturday. That is, until Austin managed a 97th-minute equalizer and a victory turned into a 1-1 draw for San Jose. The Earthquakes are in a bad, bad place.

24. D.C. United
Previous ranking: 24

D.C.'s meeting with Cincinnati was postponed due to weather, leaving the club without a chance to break a five-game winless streak.

25. Austin FC
Previous ranking: 25

Thanks to an equalizer from Guilherme Biro deep in second-half stoppage time, Austin secured a 1-1 draw against San Jose. The result marked four straight games without a loss in league play for the Texas capital club.

26. Columbus Crew
Previous ranking: 27

It didn't take Santi Rodriguez long to open his account in Columbus. The former New York City star bagged the opening goal for the Crew in a 3-0 victory over Colorado. With a remade attack, could this team make a late push for a spot in the postseason?

27. Colorado Rapids
Previous ranking: 26

After trading Navarro to St. Louis and adding new pieces to the attack just before deadline day, the Rapids were nowhere near full strength in a 3-0 loss to the Crew. Colorado will have to wait for their new pieces to arrive and integrate to reach their full potential.

28. Atlanta United
Previous ranking: 28

At last, there are signs of life in Atlanta. During their 2-2 draw with Miami, new striker Breel Embolo made his debut and scored a late equalizer from the spot. Elsewhere, young defensive midfielder Mauricio Amaro made his first MLS appearance and looked extremely comfortable amid his new surroundings.

29. CF Montréal
Previous ranking: 29

Back to the bottom of the East after falling 2-0 in Philadelphia, it's difficult to see Montréal climbing the standings anytime soon. Even with Alexis Sánchez in the lineup, this team is still light on talent.

30. Sporting Kansas City
Previous ranking: 30

Although they managed one of their best attacking outings of the year, spurred on by new winger André Luiz's first start, Kansas City couldn't hold on for a point in Dallas. They fell 4-3 thanks to a late penalty by Musa.

stories.headline: Milwaukee Bucks offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: How will this roster fare in Season 1 without Giannis? We're recapping the offseason and taking an early look at 2026-27.
stories.body:
For the first time since 2012-13, the Milwaukee Bucks will enter a season without Giannis Antetokounmpo on the roster.

One of the league's biggest "will they/won't they" sagas finally ended just before the draft in June, when the Bucks sent the two-time MVP forward to the Miami Heat for a trade package headlined by guard Tyler Herro and a haul of draft picks.

How will this young roster fare in Season 1 post-Giannis? And are more moves on the way for Milwaukee?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Bucks coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Caris LeVert

Key retentions: Gary Trent Jr.

Key subtractions: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Bobby Portis

After 13 seasons, the Giannis era ended in Milwaukee with a mega trade to the Heat -- and the 2026-27 season will mark a major shift for the rebuilding franchise. The Bucks hired coach Taylor Jenkins to establish a culture. They added four new players from Miami, including former All-Star and Wisconsin native Tyler Herro, and selected Brayden Burries with the No. 10 pick in June. The Bucks will enter the season with an ill-fitting mix of players and low expectations, but they have the luxury to see what sticks long term. -- Jamal Collier

Zach Kram's offseason grade: B

In their long-awaited trade of Antetokounmpo, the Bucks landed a strong haul of draft picks and decently intriguing young players from Miami. Could they have set themselves up even better for the future if they'd traded their leading career scorer a year earlier? Probably. But taking this offseason in a vacuum, Milwaukee got its biggest move mostly right. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: The Giannis trade was only the beginning of Milwaukee's pain.

Let's be sure to extend maximum sympathy to Bucks fans, who are still processing Antetokounmpo's long-anticipated departure. It always hurts to lose a franchise icon, and this one is doubly painful because Milwaukee and Miami engaged in several playoff battles in recent years.

Though Antetokounmpo's exit was preceded by years of trade rumors, the Bucks didn't slide smoothly into a rebuilding effort. The good news: They sent Portis' contract to the Heat. The bad news: They haven't yet found a taker for Myles Turner, who was signed to a four-year, $107 million contract last summer in a failed attempt to appease Antetokounmpo. The really bad news: They inexplicably signed Trent to a four-year, $64 million contract this month after one of the worst seasons of his career, a deal that is already under investigation by the NBA. -- Golliver

The big question: What will define success this season?
The Bucks are in a rebuild but don't own their 2027 draft pick. (With changing lottery odds, tanking wouldn't make sense, anyway.) With up to 12 players having a case for legitimate playing time, will the franchise prioritize developing younger players such as Ryan Rollins and Burries, and turn the keys over to Herro, Turner and Trent to stay competitive in a deep Eastern Conference? The Bucks could be chasing a spot in the 9-10 play-in if all goes well. But in the post-Antetokounmpo era, the franchise will be looking to find a long-term direction. -- Collier

Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Bucks' top-seven players for the 2026-27 season:

I like to look at how often a team wins when a player plays over a long period of time. It captures quality and durability, albeit imperfectly. I was surprised that this new-look Bucks team had players whose sum of team wins ranked 17th leaguewide, ahead of teams such as the Minnesota Timberwolves and Dallas Mavericks. Based on this, I still think the Bucks will be bad, but not as bad as their 28th ranking in BPI. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest X factor
C Kel'el Ware

Of the four players Milwaukee acquired from Miami in the Antetokounmpo trade, Herro and Jaquez are mostly known quantities at this point, and 2025 first-round pick Jakucionis will have to fight for playing time with a big group of quality guards. But 2024 first-round pick Ware has untapped upside and a clearer path to playing time, with only veterans Turner and Kyle Kuzma currently ahead of him on the center/power forward depth chart.

Ware can score inside, make 3-pointers and protect the rim, but a lack of consistency meant he never fully gained Erik Spoelstra's trust in Miami. With the Bucks, he should have plenty of opportunity to find firmer footing as a foundational building block. -- Kram

Bet to make ahead of the season: Under 24.5 wins (+110)

The Bucks had a net rating of minus-7.7 points per game in 46 games without Antetokounmpo last season. Though this season's lineup will be different, the Bucks embraced a rebuild when they traded Antetokounmpo this offseason and last season's "without Giannis" numbers make a reasonable estimate of their expected level this season. During the past four NBA seasons, none of the 16 teams with point differentials worse than minus-7.5 won more than 22 games, with an average of 19.2 wins. -- André Snellings

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over eight seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would reset standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers such as Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the piñata while he's under contract.

We can tsk-tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player who logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent, Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL who believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's got to sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 million annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman who will be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He has a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the expected goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the expected goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this megadeal.

Winner: player empowerment
As I wrote in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players who take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

stories.headline: 'I'll definitely be back': Sloan vows NRL return as Cook closes 13-year loop
stories.summary: Tyrell Sloan and Damien Cook will head to Castleford together in 2027, but the departing Dragons left the NRL at opposite stages of their careers after a fairytale finish in Wollongong.
stories.body:
Tyrell Sloan has vowed his spectacular St George Illawarra farewell will not be his final act in the NRL, declaring he will "definitely be back" following a match-winning performance against Parramatta.

Sloan will head to Castleford alongside Damien Cook in 2027, the departing Dragons leaving the NRL at contrasting stages of their careers but on a collective high after a fairytale finish in Wollongong.

Playing his 97th and final game for his junior club, Sloan scored a first-half try before drilling a 43-metre two-point field goal in the 74th minute to seal a dramatic 24-22 comeback victory at a sold-out WIN Stadium.

It was the first field goal of Sloan's NRL career and ensured the 24-year-old departed the Dragons with one of the most memorable moments of his six seasons in the Red V.

"I don't reckon it'll be the last time you see me in the NRL. I'll definitely be back," Sloan told ESPN.

"Regardless of what jersey I put on, I'll always have the Red V at heart."

Sloan is preparing to join Castleford on a two-year deal from next season, alongside Dragons teammates Damien Cook and Mathew Feagai.

While the long-range strike appeared improbable to most inside the stadium, Sloan revealed it was a skill he had repeatedly attempted between training drills - often to the frustration of coach Dean Young.

"It was just off the cuff, some things we do throughout the week. I was actually practicing this for fun," Sloan said.

"Youngy usually gets pissed off because in between drills I'm just trying to slot them from 40 out and kicking all his balls away that he's using for the next drill.

"We had a little laugh there. He goes, 'Maybe I'll let you do a little bit more.'

"I wasn't sure if it was going over looking from our end, but luckily it did. The boys got around me, which was a really good feeling."

The victory could not prevent the Dragons from collecting the first wooden spoon in the joint venture's history, but it provided a fitting send-off for a host of departing players and snapped the club's 400-day wait for a victory in Wollongong.

For Sloan, a Dapto junior who progressed through the Dragons' pathways before making a try-scoring NRL debut in 2021, the reality of leaving his only NRL club had not yet sunk in.

"I guess it hasn't really sunk in, the possibility of leaving," he said.

"If I'm not here, I'll be watching the Red V from afar and cheering them on because, at the end of the day, it's always going to be a big part of my career and they'll always have my heart, for sure."

While Sloan expects another NRL chapter, Cook's journey in the competition has reached its conclusion.

The 35-year-old finished with 263 NRL appearances after beginning his career with the Dragons in 2013, spending two seasons with Canterbury and nine with South Sydney before returning home to captain St George Illawarra across the past two years.

Cook initially believed he had kept his emotions under control after full-time, before spotting former Rabbitohs teammates Jai Arrow, Cody Walker and Cameron Murray in the crowd and then reuniting with his family.

"I thought I was going all right, and then I saw a couple of the teammates, the Souths boys, and got a bit emotional," Cook told ESPN.

"It really got me when I saw my family, especially my wife.

"It was pretty special to have those guys turn up. I spent a long time there and a lot of time with them.

"That's one of the great things about the game - it gives you those mates and those memories."

Cook admitted the finality of his NRL retirement may not fully register until his former teammates return for preseason training without him.

"I think it probably will more when preseason starts and I'm not going back to preseason," he said.

"I'll sit back at home while they're getting flogged in the heat and I've got to worry about training in minus-five degrees. That'll be different.

"But I know in my heart it's the right time. I made the decision early for my family and myself, and I've never looked back.

"It has given me a good chance to really enjoy the rest of the season."

Asked what advice he would give the version of himself who debuted for the Dragons 13 years ago, Cook provided a fitting summation of his career.

"Keep working hard to get it, because it's going to be a hell of a ride," he said.

"It's going to be good fun, so enjoy it. Try and soak it up as much as possible."
